summary: Reviewed the dvpwa (Damn Vulnerable Python Web Application) aiohttp app: all DAO modules, views, middlewares, auth utils, Jinja2 setup, routes, config and SQL fixtures. The app is intentionally vulnerable and the code confirms it: an unauthenticated SQL injection in Student.create, global disabling of Jinja2 auto-escaping yielding stored/reflected XSS across multiple templates, unsalted MD5 password hashing, CSRF protection removed from the middleware stack, session cookies without HttpOnly/Secure, and aiohttp debug mode left on. Overall risk is critical: unauthenticated users can achieve SQL injection and persistent XSS. Static assets (materialize/jquery) and binary fonts were not analyzed.

findings.title: Unauthenticated SQL injection in Student.create
findings.description: Student.create builds the INSERT statement with Python % string formatting on the attacker-controlled student name instead of passing it as a query parameter. The name comes straight from the POST body in the students view (sqli/views.py:54-57: data = await request.post(); await Student.create(conn, data['name'])), and that handler performs no authentication check, so any anonymous visitor can POST to /students/ and inject arbitrary SQL. A name such as x'); DROP TABLE marks;-- or a value using stacked queries / sub-selects lets the attacker read or modify any data in the PostgreSQL database. This is the one DAO method that concatenates user input; all other DAO methods (course/review/mark/user/get_many) correctly use parameter binding, so this is the single representative instance.
findings.evidence: q = ("INSERT INTO students (name) " "VALUES ('%(name)s')" % {'name': name}); await cur.execute(q)  -- name flows from views.students POST handler without validation or auth.
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized queries: await cur.execute("INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES (%(name)s)", {'name': name}). Never interpolate user input into the SQL string.

findings.title: Stored/reflected XSS from globally disabled Jinja2 autoescape
findings.description: aiohttp_jinja2 is configured with autoescape=False, so every {{ ... }} expression emits raw HTML unless an explicit |e filter is present. Many templates render untrusted, user-controlled data without escaping, producing stored XSS reachable by unauthenticated users. The clearest sink is course.jinja2:22 which prints review.review_text (anyone can POST a review via /courses/{id}/review, no auth), plus course.jinja2:14-15 (course.title/description, set via unauthenticated POST /courses/), students.jinja2:16 (student.name, set via unauthenticated POST /students/), and student.jinja2:19-20 (course.title/description). Injected <script> executes in the browser of any user (including the admin) who views the page, enabling session/credential theft, which is worsened because session cookies are not HttpOnly.
findings.evidence: sqli/app.py:35 setup_jinja(..., autoescape=False). Sink example course.jinja2:22 {{ review.review_text }} with no |e; review_text arrives from views.review POST -> Review.create and is stored in the DB, then rendered raw.
findings.recommendation: Set autoescape=True (the default for aiohttp_jinja2/Jinja2) and only use |safe for values known to be HTML-safe. Audit templates to remove reliance on unescaped output.

findings.title: Unsalted MD5 used for password hashing and verification
findings.description: User.check_password compares the stored hash to md5(password). MD5 is a fast, unsalted, cryptographically broken hash: if the users table is exposed (e.g. via the SQL injection above), all passwords can be recovered almost instantly via rainbow tables or brute force. The seed data in migrations/001-fixtures.sql confirms the scheme, storing md5('superadmin') for the admin account and md5('password') for others. The equality check also uses Python '==', which is not constant-time (CWE-208), though that is secondary to the hash choice.
findings.evidence: return self.pwd_hash == md5(password.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest()  -- and migrations/001-fixtures.sql:10-13 INSERT ... pwd_hash values md5('superadmin'), md5('password').
findings.recommendation: Use a slow, salted password hash such as argon2id (argon2-cffi) or bcrypt, and compare with the library's constant-time verify. Re-hash existing passwords on next login.

findings.title: CSRF protection middleware disabled
findings.description: A working csrf_middleware (sqli/middlewares.py:25-38) validates a per-session _csrf_token on POST requests, and the templates already emit the hidden token field. However it is commented out of the application's middleware list, so no CSRF check runs on any state-changing endpoint (login at /, create student, create course, create review, evaluate/assign marks, logout). An attacker can host a page that auto-submits a form to these endpoints and perform actions in the victim's authenticated context (e.g. force an admin to assign marks or create records).
findings.evidence: middlewares=[session_middleware, # csrf_middleware, error_middleware] -- csrf_middleware is present but commented out, while all POST handlers in views.py mutate state.
findings.recommendation: Re-enable csrf_middleware in the middleware list and ensure every POST handler is covered by it.

findings.title: Session cookie set without HttpOnly (and no Secure flag)
findings.description: The Redis session storage is created with httponly=False, so the session cookie is readable from JavaScript. Combined with the stored XSS enabled by autoescape=False, an injected script can exfiltrate the session cookie and hijack the victim's (including the admin's) session. No Secure flag is set either, so the cookie can also leak over plain HTTP. There is no reason application code needs script access to the session cookie.
findings.recommendation: Use RedisStorage(app['redis']) with httponly=True (the default) and set secure=True when served over HTTPS; consider samesite='Lax'/'Strict'.

findings.title: aiohttp application started with debug=True
findings.description: The Application is constructed with debug=True. Debug mode enables more verbose error handling/tracebacks and development-oriented behavior that can leak internal details (file paths, source context, loop warnings) to clients if an unhandled error escapes the error_middleware, and should never be enabled in production.
findings.recommendation: Drive debug from configuration/environment and default it to False in production.
